course.title: Death
course.about: There is one thing I can be sure of: I am going to die. But what am I to make of that fact? This course will examine a number of issues that arise once we begin to reflect on our mortality. The possibility that death may not actually be the end is considered. Are we, in some sense, immortal? Would immortality be desirable? Also a clearer notion of what it is to die is examined. What does it mean to say that a person has died? What kind of fact is that? And, finally, different attitudes to death are evaluated. Is death an evil? How? Why? Is suicide morally permissible? Is it rational? How should the knowledge that I am going to die affect the way I live my life?

bites.body: Two more views regarding the metaphysical key to personal identity are discussed: the body view and the personality view.

bites.body: According to the body view, an individual is identified in terms of his or her physical body.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward

bites.headline: Personal Identity, Part III: Objections to the Personality Theory

bites.headline: The

bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward

bites.body: The personality theory is revised to state that the key to personal identity is having the same personality provided that there is no branching, that is, provided there is no transfer or duplication of the same personality from one body to another.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: In answering this question, attention is first drawn to the bodily and mental functions that are crucial in defining the moment of death.

bites.body: In trying to further access how people think about death, Professor Kagan explores the claim that "we all die alone," presents a variety of arguments against it and ends by considering whether the primary badness of death could lie in the…

bites.headline: The Badness of Death, Part II: The Deprivation Account
bites.body: This lecture continues to explore the issue of why death may be bad.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: This
bites.body: According to the deprivation account, what is bad about death is the fact that because one ceases to exist, one becomes deprived of the good things in life.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Being dead is not intrinsically bad; it is comparatively bad and one is worse off only by virtue of not being able to enjoy the things one enjoyed while alive, such as watching the sunset, listening to music, and discussing philosophy.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: The Badness of Death, Part III; Immortality, Part I
bites.body: The discussion of the badness of death continues by asking whether it is bad that we do not exist before our birth.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: The
bites.body: The views of a number of contemporary philosophers, such as Tom Nagle, Fred Feldman, and Derek Parfit, are introduced.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: The lecture concludes with Bernard Williams' take on immortality which posits that no kind of human life can continue to be enjoyable and attractive for eternity.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Immortality Part II; The Value of Life, Part I
bites.body: The lecture begins with further exploration of the question of whether it is desirable to live forever under the right circumstances, and then turns to consideration of some alternative theories of the nature of well-being.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: The
bites.body: One popular theory is hedonism, but the thought experiment of being on an "experience machine" suggests that this view may be inadequate.

bites.body: Lecture 20 continues the discussion of the value of life.

bites.headline: Lecture
bites.body: It considers the neutral container theory, which holds that the value of life is simply a function of its contents, both pleasant and painful, and contrasts this with the valuable container theory, which assigns value to being…
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Among the issues addressed are the inevitability, variability and unpredictability of death.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Other Bad Aspects of Death, Part II
bites.body: Further bad aspects of death are considered, including ubiquity, or the fact that death may occur at any time and strike anyone.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Further
bites.body: Professor Kagan invites students to contemplate the possibility of death-free time periods, vacation spots, and activities.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
